# Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of dermatitis herpetiformis

## Abstract

<mark>Dermatitis herpetiformis is a rare disease that should be considered the cutaneous expression of a gluten-sensitive enteropathy indistinguishable from celiac disease.</mark> <mark>Dermatitis herpetiformis is often misdiagnosed, and to date, no guidelines for its management have been published in the literature.</mark> These guidelines have been developed for dermatologists by the Group for Cutaneous Immunopathology of the Italian Society of Dermatology and Venereology. They reflect the best available evidence at the time of preparation, along with the clinical experience of the authors and members of the Italian Group for Cutaneous Immunopathology.

<mark>The diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis is established through clinical, histological, immunopathological, and serological evaluation.</mark> <mark>A gluten-free diet (GFD) is the treatment of choice.</mark> <mark>Dapsone and/or other medications may be used during the initial phase until the GFD becomes effective.</mark> These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis and management of dermatitis herpetiformis.

## Keywords

celiac disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, diagnosis, guidelines, management, therapy

## Introduction

<mark>Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease characterized by pruritic, polymorphic skin lesions and distinct histopathological and immunopathological features.</mark> <mark>Increasing evidence supports that dermatitis herpetiformis represents the cutaneous manifestation of a gluten-sensitive enteropathy identical to celiac disease.</mark> <mark>Both conditions are multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition and environmental triggers, resulting in specific pathology in the small intestine and skin, respectively.</mark>

<mark>There is a strong association with HLA-DQ2 (present in 80–90% of patients) and HLA-DQ8 (in 10–20% of patients), which is shared by both dermatitis herpetiformis and celiac disease.</mark>

<mark>The disease typically manifests in the third decade of life, although it can occur at any age.</mark> <mark>It predominantly affects Caucasians.</mark> The reported incidence is 11.5 per 100,000 in Scotland and ranges from 19.6 to 39.2 per 100,000 in Sweden.

Patients with dermatitis herpetiformis have an increased risk of immunomediated diseases and associated conditions, including lymphoma.

## Diagnostic Protocol

Clear and concise diagnostic criteria are essential for accurate identification of dermatitis herpetiformis, ensuring appropriate treatment and long-term monitoring.

<mark>Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation, histology, immunopathology—specifically direct immunofluorescence (DIF)—and serology, including IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) and IgA endomysial antibodies (EMA).</mark>

While a suggestive clinical picture and positive serologic tests support the diagnosis—and some authors consider anti-tTG testing sufficient—DIF of perilesional (uninvolved) skin remains the gold standard for confirming dermatitis herpetiformis.

In cases of negative DIF results, serial sectioning of the biopsy specimen should be performed. If results remain negative, a second biopsy should be obtained from clearly uninvolved skin, ensuring the patient is not following a gluten-free diet, which may affect test outcomes. Given that false-negative IgA detection is often due to technical issues, DIF should be performed in experienced laboratories to reduce the risk of both false-positive and false-negative results.

# Other dietary recommendations

<mark>The gluten-free diet (GFD) is the foundation of therapy for dermatitis herpetiformis (DH).</mark> <mark>However, patients should avoid excessive iodine intake (e.g., seafood, multivitamin-multimicronutrient supplements) as it may trigger disease relapses, particularly in those on an incomplete GFD.</mark>

# Dapsone

<mark>Dapsone is the first-line drug for symptomatic treatment of DH.</mark> <mark>Although no randomized controlled trials have evaluated its efficacy—except for small case series—there is strong consensus that dapsone is highly effective.</mark> <mark>It remains the most effective treatment for cutaneous symptoms and pruritus until the GFD takes full effect, which may take 6–24 months.</mark> <mark>Skin lesions and itching typically resolve within 3–4 days of starting dapsone, and symptoms usually recur within days of discontinuation.</mark>

<mark>Before initiating dapsone, serum glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH) activity should be assessed to rule out deficiency and prevent hemolytic anemia.</mark> <mark>The starting dose depends on symptom severity.</mark> <mark>A low-dose regimen begins at 25 mg once or twice daily to minimize side effects, with weekly increments of 25 mg until an effective dose is reached, up to a maximum of 200 mg/day.</mark> <mark>For maintenance, a dose of 0.5–1 mg/kg/day is generally sufficient to control pruritus and prevent new lesions.</mark>

# Dietary counselling

All DH patients should be referred to a dietitian to ensure proper implementation of a gluten-free diet, especially if additional dietary modifications are required due to comorbidities.

# <mark>Indications of dapsone treatment in DH patients</mark>

Dapsone therapy is indicated in the following situations:

- <mark>Intolerable or severe skin involvement</mark>  
- <mark>Skin manifestations persist despite a strict GFD</mark>  
- <mark>Patient is unwilling or unable to adhere to a GFD</mark>  

In cases of severe disease and intense pruritus, higher starting doses (e.g., 50 mg twice or three times daily) may be used, provided G6PDH deficiency has been excluded. Once clinical remission is achieved, the dose should be tapered to the lowest effective maintenance level. If no improvement is observed within one week at a dose ≥150 mg/day, the diagnosis should be re-evaluated or alternative therapies considered. A strict and sustained GFD allows for rapid reduction of dapsone dosage, and in most patients, dapsone can eventually be discontinued entirely.

For pediatric patients, the initial dose is 1–2 mg/kg orally once daily or in two divided doses, with a maximum single dose of 50 mg. The maintenance dose is individualized and typically ranges from 10–25% of the initial effective dose.

No dose adjustment is necessary in renal impairment. In hepatic impairment, caution is advised, and regular laboratory monitoring is recommended.

Dapsone therapy should continue until complete remission is achieved. In case of relapse, the dose may be temporarily increased by the patient under medical guidance. If a severe relapse occurs after discontinuation, dapsone can be safely restarted.

# Dapsone

<mark>Dapsone is a valid therapeutic option for dermatitis herpetiformis during the 1- to 2-year period required for a gluten-free diet (GFD) to become fully effective.</mark> <mark>A dosage of 1 mg/kg/day can control itching and blister formation.</mark> <mark>Although dapsone effectively reduces pruritus and inflammatory skin lesions, patients must be closely monitored—particularly for renal and liver function—due to the risk of severe adverse effects.</mark> <mark>The most common side effect is hemolysis, and patients should be evaluated within 2 weeks of starting therapy, as hemolysis can be acute in some individuals.</mark>

<mark>Adverse reactions to dapsone are classified as either toxic or idiosyncratic and are typically dose-dependent.</mark> <mark>They are more frequent in patients with comorbidities such as anemia, cardiopulmonary disease, or glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.</mark> <mark>Dapsone can also induce a severe hypersensitivity syndrome in approximately 5% of dermatitis herpetiformis patients, occurring 2–6 weeks after treatment initiation.</mark> <mark>This syndrome includes fever, rash, malaise, lymphadenopathy, and variable visceral involvement.</mark>

## Table 4: Main adverse reactions to dapsone  
- **Toxic reactions**:  
  - Hemolysis  
  - Methemoglobinemia  
  - Dose-dependent hepatotoxicity  
  - Peripheral neuropathy  

- **Idiosyncratic reactions**:  
  - Hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS)  
  - Agranulocytosis  
  - Hepatitis  
  - Skin rashes  

---

## Table 5: Indications for monitoring  
- GFD adherence  
- Possible development of autoimmune associated diseases (despite GFD adherence)  
- Metabolic alterations (dyslipidemia, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis)  
- Possible development of neoplastic (e.g., lymphoma) or non-neoplastic complications (e.g., refractory celiac disease, ulcerative jejunoileitis, collagenous sprue)  

---

## Table 6: Item list for routine check-ups  
- Physical examination  
- Dietician counselling  
- Serological laboratory tests:  
  - Hemochrome  
  - Malabsorption evaluation (sideremia, ferritin levels, mean corpuscular volume, glucose, thyroid hormones)  
- Immunological and autoimmune markers (dermatitis herpetiformis-specific and non-specific autoantibodies)  

---

# Sulfasalazine and Sulphamethoxypyridazine

Sulfasalazine and sulphamethoxypyridazine may serve as effective alternatives to dapsone, particularly when dapsone is ineffective or associated with adverse events. The recommended dosages are 1–2 g/day for sulfasalazine and 0.25–1.5 g/day for sulphamethoxypyridazine.

Both drugs share similar adverse effects, including hypersensitivity reactions, hemolytic anemia, proteinuria, and crystalluria. Therefore, a complete blood count with differential and urine microscopy with urinalysis should be performed before treatment initiation and monthly for the first 3 months, then every 6 months thereafter. The most common adverse effects—nausea, anorexia, and vomiting—can often be minimized by using enteric-coated formulations.

---

# Corticosteroids

Oral corticosteroids are generally ineffective in dermatitis herpetiformis. However, topical application of potent or very potent corticosteroids, such as clobetasol propionate, can help reduce pruritus and skin inflammation.

---

# Antihistamines

Although antihistamines have limited efficacy in dermatitis herpetiformis, third-generation agents with specific activity on eosinophilic granulocytes may be considered a third-line treatment option for symptom control, particularly for pruritus and itching.

---

# Dermatitis Herpetiformis Monitoring

Regular follow-up is essential to confirm diagnosis through objective response to a gluten-free diet and to identify non-compliance. Patients with dermatitis herpetiformis and associated celiac disease should be evaluated at regular intervals—initially 6 months after diagnosis and then annually—by a multidisciplinary healthcare team including a physician and a dietician.

# <mark>Cutaneous Anthrax</mark>

<mark>Spores are infectious particles that revert to active bacillary form in host tissues.</mark> <mark>*Bacillus anthracis* is a natural pathogen of livestock, particularly sheep, goats, and cattle.</mark> Most human cases are occupationally related, occurring after exposure to infected animals or animal products.

## <mark>Clinical Features</mark>

<mark>**Cutaneous anthrax** is the most common form of the disease and is associated with the lowest morbidity compared to inhalational and gastrointestinal anthrax, which are more virulent and frequently fatal.</mark>

### <mark>Cutaneous Lesions</mark>
<mark>Cutaneous anthrax occurs when spores enter minor breaks in the skin, typically on exposed areas such as the hands, face, or legs.</mark> <mark>The infection begins as a painless papule at the site of inoculation, often resembling an insect bite.</mark> <mark>Over several days, the lesion progresses through stages:</mark>

- <mark>**Papular** → **Vesicular** → **Hemorrhagic bulla with central necrosis** → **Eschar formation**</mark>

<mark>The lesion enlarges and becomes surrounded by marked, brawny, non-pitting edema ("malignant edema").</mark> <mark>A glistening pseudobulla develops, which becomes hemorrhagic and may appear umbilicated.</mark> <mark>Central necrosis leads to a characteristic jet-black eschar.</mark>

- <mark>The ulcer is typically **painless**, a key feature distinguishing it from conditions like brown recluse spider bites.</mark>
- <mark>Satellite papules or vesicles may appear, sometimes spreading along lymphatics in a sporotrichoid pattern.</mark>
- <mark>True pustules are rare; the term "malignant pustule" is a misnomer, as the lesion does not suppurate.</mark>

<mark>One or more lesions may develop depending on the inoculation route.</mark> <mark>Regional lymphadenitis, fever, malaise, and chills are common, potentially leading to an ulcero-glandular syndrome.</mark>

<mark>Lesion progression is driven by bacterial toxins and continues despite antibiotic therapy.</mark> <mark>The eschar dries and separates within 1 to 2 weeks if untreated, but appropriate treatment prevents systemic complications.</mark>

### <mark>Systemic Findings</mark>
<mark>Cutaneous anthrax may be accompanied by:</mark>
- Fever
- <mark>Tachycardia</mark>
- <mark>Hypotension</mark>
- <mark>Tender regional lymphadenopathy</mark>

## <mark>Histopathology</mark>
<mark>Key histopathologic findings include:</mark>
- <mark>Hemorrhagic edema</mark>
- <mark>Dilated lymphatics</mark>
- <mark>Epidermal necrosis</mark>
- <mark>Sparse inflammatory infiltrate (due to toxin-mediated immune suppression)</mark>
- <mark>Bacilli may be visible in the eschar</mark>
- <mark>Immunohistochemical stains can aid diagnosis</mark>

## Treatment
- <mark>**Naturally occurring anthrax**: Treated with **penicillin** or **doxycycline**.</mark>
- <mark>**Bioterrorism-associated (weaponized) anthrax**: Initial treatment should include a **fluoroquinolone** (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) due to potential resistance to penicillin and tetracyclines. This recommendation applies even to pregnant women and children.</mark>
  <mark>- Once susceptibility is confirmed, therapy may be adjusted accordingly.</mark>

**Note**: Antibiotics kill vegetative bacilli but do not neutralize toxins already produced. Therefore, tissue damage may progress despite effective antimicrobial treatment.

## Important Notes
- *Bacillus anthracis* is classified by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as a **Category A bioterrorism agent** due to its potential for aerosolization.
- There is **no human-to-human transmission** of anthrax.

# POSITION STATEMENT

## <mark>Position statement: LEPROSY: Diagnosis, treatment and follow-up</mark>

### Abstract

<mark>Background: Leprosy, or Hansen's disease, is a chronic infection caused by *Mycobacterium leprae* (M.</mark> leprae) or *Mycobacterium lepromatosis* (M. <mark>lepromatosis).</mark> <mark>In Europe, most leprosy cases are imported, although occasional cases arise from old endemic foci.</mark> <mark>The disease is often not suspected due to its diminished emphasis in medical education.</mark> In the late 20th century, global health priorities shifted toward tuberculosis and HIV, leading to a reduction in the WHO leprosy programme under the assumption that leprosy was nearly eliminated. <mark>This lack of awareness contributes to harmful diagnostic delays.</mark>

### Introduction

<mark>Leprosy, also known as Hansen’s disease, is a chronic infection caused by *Mycobacterium leprae* or *Mycobacterium lepromatosis*.</mark> While most cases in Europe are imported, sporadic cases continue to emerge from historical endemic areas. <mark>The condition is frequently overlooked because it is no longer a focus in medical training.</mark> During the late twentieth century, attention shifted to tuberculosis (TB) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), resulting in a scaling down of the WHO leprosy programme based on the belief that leprosy had been largely eradicated.

In 2005, the WHO declared leprosy eliminated as a public health problem globally. However, this declaration was premature. To date, approximately 250,000 new cases are reported annually worldwide, with stable incidence and prevalence rates. <mark>With increasing migration from endemic regions, the risk of leprosy in Europe is rising.</mark> Current immigrant populations often live in overcrowded and suboptimal conditions—factors that may facilitate transmission, unlike earlier migration patterns.

Patients are now being diagnosed across the Western world, often after significant diagnostic delays, leading to lifelong disabilities. Medical curricula provide minimal coverage of leprosy, leaving even specialists such as dermatologists, neurologists, and rheumatologists poorly equipped to recognize it. <mark>Lack of awareness remains a primary reason for missed diagnoses.</mark> This position statement aims to improve physician awareness and understanding of leprosy in the European context.

### <mark>Diagnosis</mark>

<mark>Leprosy primarily affects the peripheral nerves, skin, and mucosa—especially the upper respiratory tract.</mark> <mark>Skin lesions are typically the first noticeable sign, contributing to its classification as a dermatological condition.</mark> <mark>If untreated, leprosy can lead to permanent damage to the skin, nerves, limbs, and eyes.</mark> Tissue damage results partly from direct *M. <mark>leprae* infiltration, but the majority of pathology arises from immunological reactions.</mark>

Secondary infections due to trauma—following sensory loss—can lead to tissue destruction. Bone and cartilage resorption may occur, resulting in shortening and deformities of fingers, toes, and the nose (clinical features illustrated in deformed hands due to nerve damage and secondary infection).

<mark>Patients may report:</mark>
- Loss of sensation in skin lesions, hands, or feet
- Aches and pains in the face or limbs
- Numbness, "sleepy" or "dead" feelings
- Paresthesias described as "ants running under the skin" in affected areas

Skin lesions typically present as hypopigmented or erythematous macules, papules, nodules, or plaques, which may be skin-colored or slightly red.

<mark>Clinically, leprosy is diagnosed when a patient exhibits at least two of the three cardinal signs.</mark> However, in endemic areas, the WHO considers the presence of a single cardinal sign sufficient for diagnosis—though this approach sometimes overlooks nerve enlargement.

The three well-established cardinal signs of leprosy (recognized for over 100 years) are:

1. **Loss of sensation in a skin lesion**  
2. **Enlarged peripheral nerve**  
3. **Positive skin smears**

Currently, there are no specific laboratory tests to confirm leprosy. Available tests support classification, monitoring, and detection of relapse but are not diagnostic on their own.

Sensory loss is assessed using a wisp of cotton wool. The test involves gentle touch (not brushing) of the lesion and surrounding skin to evaluate perception.

## Classification and Clinical Forms of Leprosy

<mark>Leprosy may resolve spontaneously (in many cases) or progress into one of the clinical types described in the **Ridley-Jopling classification**, depending on the development of cell-mediated immunity (CMI).</mark> Another challenging group is **pure neural leprosy**, characterized by nerve involvement without skin lesions. Its reported frequency ranges from 1 to 10%, varying by geographic region and level of clinical awareness.

For field use, the **World Health Organization (WHO)** simplifies classification based on the number of skin lesions:
- <mark>**Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy**: Five or fewer skin lesions.</mark>
- **Multibacillary (MB) leprosy**: More than five skin lesions.

While this system is practical, studies indicate that up to 30% of patients may be misclassified as PB using this method alone, leading to potential undertreatment.

---

## Treatment

The earliest documented treatment with modest efficacy was **chaulmoogra oil**, referenced in the *Sushruta Samhita* (600 BC). Though effects were limited, some benefit was observed in paucibacillary cases.

<mark>The first effective antimicrobial therapy emerged in 1943 with **promin**, an intravenous sulfone.</mark> <mark>This was soon followed by the introduction of **dapsone (diaminodiphenylsulfone, DDS)**, an oral sulfone that became the standard of care.</mark> <mark>However, by the 1970s, **dapsone resistance** became widespread.</mark> <mark>With the availability of **rifampicin (RMP)**, combination therapy was advocated to prevent resistance.</mark>

<mark>In 1982, the **WHO Chemotherapy Study Group** formally recommended multidrug therapy (MDT), combining **rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine**, depending on classification.</mark>

<mark>Today, **WHO-recommended multidrug therapy (MDT)** remains the global standard and is widely implemented.</mark>

---

## Multidrug Therapy (MDT) Regimens

### Paucibacillary Leprosy (PB)
- <mark>**Rifampicin**: 600 mg, once monthly under supervision for 6 months.</mark>
- <mark>**Dapsone**: 100 mg daily, unsupervised.</mark>

<mark>For a 60 kg adult, treatment can be discontinued after **6 supervised monthly doses administered within 9 months**.</mark>

A recent proposal suggests adding **clofazimine (Lamprene)** to the 6-month PB regimen to reduce undertreatment and harmonize therapy across classifications. This approach aims to minimize reliance on clinical classification, though it remains under debate among clinicians.

---

### Multibacillary Leprosy (MB)
- <mark>**Monthly (supervised)**: 600 mg rifampicin + 300 mg clofazimine (Lamprene).</mark>
- <mark>**Daily (unsupervised)**: 100 mg dapsone + 50 mg clofazimine.</mark>

<mark>The official WHO recommendation is **12 supervised monthly doses within 18 months**.</mark> However, many clinicians modify this:
- **Low bacterial index (BI)**: 12 monthly doses over 18 months.
- **High bacterial index (BI ≥ 4)**: 24 monthly doses over 36 months.

Doses are standardized for a 60 kg patient.

---

## Uniform MDT (U-MDT)

The WHO is currently evaluating **Uniform MDT (U-MDT)** — a **6-month regimen using rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine for all leprosy patients**, regardless of classification. This approach eliminates the need for classification.

However, this proposal is **controversial** and faces strong opposition from many clinicians due to concerns about undertreating multibacillary cases.

---

## Treatment Outcomes and Safety Considerations

- The established MDT regimens have proven highly effective, with **relapse rates below 4%**.
- However, **follow-up duration for MB leprosy is often insufficient**, raising concerns about late relapses.
- **Dapsone-related haemolysis** is a known risk, particularly in **Nordic Caucasians**, even in the absence of G6PD deficiency. Reducing the dose to **50 mg daily** maintains efficacy while significantly reducing anaemia, likely due to genetic factors.
- <mark>**Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome** is more common in **Nepalese and Chinese patients**, requiring heightened clinical vigilance.</mark>

## <mark>Uniform MDT (U-MDT) and Current Treatment Recommendations</mark>

<mark>At present, the WHO recommends **Uniform MDT (U-MDT)** — a 6-month treatment with **rifampicin (RMP), dapsone, and clofazimine** — for all forms of leprosy, regardless of classification.</mark> <mark>This approach eliminates the need to differentiate between paucibacillary (PB) and multibacillary (MB) disease.</mark> <mark>However, this recommendation is controversial and has been questioned and strongly opposed by many clinicians.</mark>

## <mark>Efficacy and Safety of MDT Components</mark>

<mark>The traditional MDT regimens have demonstrated high efficacy with very low relapse rates (approximately 4%).</mark> <mark>However, in multibacillary leprosy, follow-up periods are often too short to fully assess long-term outcomes.</mark>

### <mark>Dapsone Considerations</mark>
- <mark>**Caution is advised with dapsone use in Nordic Caucasians**, who are prone to haemolysis even with normal G6PD status.</mark>
- <mark>A reduced dose of **50 mg daily** appears effective in most patients and significantly reduces the risk of anaemia, likely due to genetic factors.</mark>
- <mark>**Nepalese and Chinese patients** have an increased risk of developing **dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome** and require careful monitoring.</mark>

## <mark>Alternative Regimens</mark>

### Single-Lesion Leprosy
For single-lesion paucibacillary leprosy, a **single-dose regimen** of **rifampicin, ofloxacin, and minocycline (ROM)** was previously advocated. While convenient, this regimen proved less effective than standard WHO-MDT.

### Monthly ROM Regimen
ROM was also tested as a monthly regimen for both tuberculoid and lepromatous leprosy but showed inferior efficacy compared to WHO-recommended MDT.

---

## Table 1: WHO-Recommended Treatment of Leprosy

<mark>| Age group | Drug | Dosage and frequency | Duration (MB) | Duration (PB) |</mark>
<mark>|---------|------|------------------------|---------------|---------------|</mark>
<mark>| Adult | Rifampicin | 600 mg once a month | 12 months | 6 months |</mark>
<mark>| | Clofazimine | 300 mg once a month and 50 mg daily | | |</mark>

<mark>| | Clofazimine | 6 mg/kg once a month and 1 mg/kg daily | | |</mark>

## Viral Infections and Pathogenesis of PCT

<mark>There is a well-documented association between porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, as well as combined HCV and HIV infections.</mark> <mark>The exact role of these viral infections in the pathogenesis of PCT remains unclear.</mark> Some studies have suggested a possible interaction with the **HFE gene mutation H63D**, although it is also plausible that the association is secondary to non-specific hepatotoxic effects of the viruses rather than a direct causative role.

## Multifactorial Pathogenesis

The known effects of alcohol, estrogens, chlorinated hydrocarbons, iron overload, and viral infections on the heme biosynthetic pathway indicate that each of these factors can contribute to the excessive hepatic porphyrinogenesis observed in PCT. Hepatic siderosis (iron accumulation in the liver) appears to be a critical pathological endpoint in PCT. It is hypothesized that these various factors intensify the ability of iron to inhibit **UROGEN decarboxylase**, particularly by attacking its catalytic site. 

Thus, the clinical expression of PCT results from the interplay of multiple genetic and environmental factors. Importantly, unlike in the acute porphyrias, drugs known to induce acute neurovisceral attacks do not typically trigger similar neurological crises in PCT.

## <mark>Clinical Manifestations</mark>

<mark>Cutaneous manifestations of PCT are characterized by **vesicles and bullae** that progress to erosions and crusting, primarily in areas prone to trauma—most commonly the **dorsa of the hands** (Fig.</mark> 132-8). <mark>Skin fragility is a hallmark feature.</mark> <mark>As lesions heal, scarring may occur, and **milia**—small, pearly white to yellow cysts—frequently develop, especially on the fingers and hands.</mark> <mark>These skin findings are shared among the hepatic porphyrias with photosensitivity: **PCT, variegate porphyria (VP), and hereditary coproporphyria (HCP)**.</mark>

<mark>Although lesions predominantly affect sun-exposed areas, patients often do not recognize sunlight as a trigger, since the intense, painful photosensitivity seen in erythropoietic porphyrias is uncommon in PCT.</mark> <mark>However, many patients report seasonal variation, with worsening in spring and summer and improvement in fall and winter—consistent with increased porphyrin excretion during warmer months.</mark>

### Additional Dermatological Features

- **Pigmentary changes**: Hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation may occur, often mottled and resembling **chloasma**.
- **Facial suffusion**: A purplish-red ("**heliotrope**") discoloration may appear on the central face, particularly around the periorbital regions. This finding can mimic the facial plethora seen in **polycythemia rubra vera** (Fig. 132-9) and is not observed in porphyrias of bone marrow origin.
- **Hypertrichosis**: Non-virilizing excessive hair growth, particularly on the face and temples, is a distinctive feature that often prompts female patients to seek dermatological evaluation (Fig. 132-10).

# Hepatitis C

The majority of cases of posttransfusion hepatitis have been due to hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. However, widespread screening of blood products has dramatically reduced the incidence of new infections.

<mark>Cutaneous manifestations associated with acute and chronic HCV infection include:</mark>
- <mark>**Leukocytoclastic vasculitis**, typically secondary to **cryoglobulinemia**</mark>
- <mark>Cutaneous necrosis</mark>
- <mark>Pruritus</mark>
- <mark>Acquired angioedema</mark>
- <mark>**Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT)**</mark>
- Erythema nodosum
- Urticaria
- Erythema multiforme
- Polyarteritis nodosa

**Lichen planus** is more frequently observed in patients with HCV infection, although reported incidence rates vary across studies. In Italian patients with HCV-associated oral lichen planus, there is an increased frequency of the **HLA-DR6 allele**, suggesting a potential role for host genetic factors in this association.

---

## Disorders of Both Skin and Liver

The following conditions are characterized by concurrent involvement of the skin and liver:

### Argininosuccinic Aciduria
- Autosomal recessive disorder
- Features include ataxia, seizures, severe intellectual disability, hepatomegaly with liver dysfunction, and brittle hair

### Dermatomyositis
- May be the initial presentation of a primary or secondary hepatic tumor

### Eruptive Neonatal Angiomatosis
- Characterized by multiple cutaneous angiomas
- Vascular lesions may also affect internal organs, including the liver

### Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD)
- Both acute and chronic forms can significantly affect the skin and liver
- Most commonly seen in patients following bone marrow transplantation

### Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu Disease)
- Arteriovenous fistulas lead to vascular shunting
- Hepatic involvement may manifest as multiple small telangiectatic vessels, resembling cirrhosis

### Histiocytoses
- Includes **Langerhans cell histiocytosis** and **malignant histiocytosis**
- Both skin and liver can be involved

### Immunodeficiency States
- Predispose to infections affecting both skin and liver
- Examples:

- Group of metabolic disorders with both cutaneous and hepatic manifestations:

  - **Erythropoietic (erythrohepatic) porphyria**

### Syphilis
- Hepatic granulomas can occur

- Most often due to **drug-induced hepatitis**
- Thrombotic complications such as **Budd-Chiari syndrome** and **veno-occlusive disease** may occur, with or without lupus anticoagulant

# <mark>Hepatoerythropoietic Porphyria (HEP)</mark>

## <mark>CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS</mark>
<mark>In some patients, liver function test results have been abnormal, but serum iron and iron binding are normal.</mark> The clinical manifestations of HEP resemble a combination of those seen in Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT) and Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria (CEP).

## <mark>LABORATORY FINDINGS</mark>
<mark>The urinary porphyrin pattern in HEP is similar to that observed in PCT.</mark> However, elevated red blood cell (RBC) protoporphyrin (PROTO) levels help distinguish HEP from PCT. <mark>Characteristic findings in HEP include:</mark>

- <mark>Elevated urinary uroporphyrin I and III (URO-COPRO ratio > 5:1)</mark>
- <mark>Urinary 7-carboxyl porphyrins with more than 90% as isomer III</mark>
- <mark>Increased fecal coproporphyrin (COPRO) and isocoproporphyrin (ISOCOPRO)</mark>
- Elevated RBC PROTO (zinc-chelated)

<mark>These findings indicate abnormal porphyrin synthesis in both the liver and the bone marrow.</mark> <mark>In contrast to PCT, serum iron concentrations are typically normal in HEP.</mark>

## HISTOPATHOLOGY
Skin biopsy specimens from blistering lesions show subepidermal bullae, similar to those seen in PCT. Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive material is present in and around dermal capillaries. However, skin biopsy is not required for diagnosis.

## <mark>DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</mark>
Conditions to consider include:
- Childhood porphyrias (e.g., homozygous or compound heterozygous variants of Variegate Porphyria [VP] and Hereditary Coproporphyria [HCP])
- Severe forms of PCT
- <mark>Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria (CEP)</mark>

<mark>Unlike HEP, CEP is associated with erythrodontia and mutilating skin scarring.</mark>

## TREATMENT
There is no specific treatment for HEP other than strict photoprotection to prevent skin damage.

---

# Pseudoporphyria

Pseudoporphyria refers to a condition in which patients exhibit cutaneous symptoms resembling PCT but lack the characteristic porphyrin abnormalities.

## ETIOLOGY
It may be induced by certain medications, including:
- Furosemide
- Nalidixic acid
- Tetracycline
- Naproxen
- Pyridoxine
- Isotretinoin

It can also occur in patients with chronic renal failure undergoing long-term hemodialysis. In these cases, plasma porphyrin levels may be moderately elevated (2- to 4-fold) due to impaired renal clearance and inadequate removal by dialysis filters.

## HISTOPATHOLOGY
- Blistering is subepidermal with minimal or no dermal inflammation
- PAS staining shows little or no deposition around upper dermal blood vessels
- Indirect immunofluorescence on split skin reveals no dermal deposition of fluorescent material
- Direct immunofluorescence may show patchy granular deposition of IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone — a finding also seen in PCT and epidermolysis bullosa acquisita

---

# Erythropoietic Protoporphyria (EPP)

## AT A GLANCE
- Second most common cutaneous porphyria
- Autosomal dominant inheritance with deficiency of ferrochelatase
- Onset typically in early childhood (1–4 years); late onset is rare
- Cutaneous manifestations: erythema, edema, purpura, skin thickening, waxy scars; blistering is uncommon
- Symptoms: acute burning and stinging of the skin, often severe
- Approximately 5% of patients may develop potentially fatal hepatic failure

# PRIMARY CUTANEOUS T-CELL LYMPHOMAS

<mark>Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCLs) are non-Hodgkin lymphomas characterized by a dominant skin-homing T-cell clone.</mark> <mark>They account for approximately 80% of all cutaneous lymphomas.</mark> <mark>The most common subtypes are mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary syndrome (SS), with an annual incidence of three to four new cases per million people.</mark> After MF and SS, the primary cutaneous CD30+ lymphoproliferative disorders—including lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP) and primary cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma (cALCL)—represent the second most common group of CTCLs, comprising approximately 30% of cases.

An understanding of the unique epidermal sanctuary that harbors, preserves, and perpetuates CTCL is essential for comprehending disease persistence and recurrence.

# <mark>Mycosis Fungoides</mark>

## <mark>DEFINITION</mark>

<mark>Mycosis fungoides (MF) is the most frequent variant of CTCL, typically presenting in mid to late adulthood (median age at diagnosis, 55 to 60 years), with a male-to-female ratio of 2:1.</mark>

## <mark>CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: Skin Signs</mark>

<mark>MF is clinically categorized into patch, plaque, and tumor stages, although patients may exhibit more than one type of lesion simultaneously.</mark>

### <mark>Patch Stage</mark>
<mark>In early patch-stage MF, patients present with single or multiple erythematous, scaly macules and patches of variable size, usually well-demarcated.</mark> <mark>Lesion color ranges from orange to dusky violet-red.</mark> <mark>The distribution typically favors non-sun-exposed areas, with early involvement of the "bathing trunk" region and intertriginous zones.</mark> <mark>The eruption may be intensely pruritic or asymptomatic and can occasionally be transient, resolving spontaneously without scarring.</mark>

<mark>Diagnosis at this stage is often challenging.</mark> <mark>Many patients report a history of "chronic dermatitis" lasting 10 to 20 years, previously misdiagnosed as contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, or eczema.</mark> <mark>In any case of therapy-resistant dermatosis, multiple skin biopsies should be performed to evaluate for MF.</mark>

### <mark>Plaque Stage</mark>
<mark>Patches may persist for months or years before progressing to plaques, or plaques may arise de novo.</mark> <mark>Plaques are sharply demarcated, scaly, elevated lesions that are dusky red to violaceous and variably indurated.</mark> <mark>Annular, arcuate, or serpiginous configurations with central atrophy and active disease at the periphery are characteristic.</mark> <mark>Central clearing may occur, leaving poikiloderma—comprising atrophy, telangiectasia, and pigmentary changes (hyper- or hypopigmentation).</mark>

### <mark>Tumor Stage</mark>
<mark>Tumors may develop anywhere but show a predilection for the face and body folds—such as the axillae, groin, antecubital fossae, and, in women, the inframammary area.</mark> <mark>Tumors may arise within pre-existing patches or plaques, indicating a vertical growth phase.</mark> <mark>This transition reflects more biologically aggressive behavior, with neoplastic cells expanding vertically through the dermis, leading to rapidly enlarging nodules or tumors.</mark>

## Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma (CTCL) and Extracorporeal Photopheresis (ECP)

### Which patients should be considered for ECP treatment?

<mark>Extracorporeal photopheresis (ECP) should be considered for patients with **cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL)**, particularly in the following settings:</mark>

- <mark>**Sézary syndrome (SS)**: ECP is a first-line systemic therapy for patients with leukemic involvement, given its ability to target circulating malignant T-cells.</mark>
- <mark>**Advanced-stage mycosis fungoides (MF)**: Patients with stage IIB–IV disease, especially those with blood involvement (e.g., B1 or B2 according to the ISCL/EORTC staging) or extensive skin burden (e.g., erythroderma), are strong candidates for ECP.</mark>
- <mark>**Early-stage MF (IB–IIA) with refractory or progressive disease**: ECP may be used when skin-directed therapies have failed or are not feasible.</mark>
- <mark>**Patients with erythroderma**: ECP is particularly effective in managing erythrodermic CTCL, regardless of Sézary cell count.</mark>
- <mark>**Combination therapy settings**: ECP is often combined with other systemic agents (e.g., retinoids like bexarotene, interferon-alpha, or monoclonal antibodies such as mogamulizumab) to enhance efficacy.</mark>

<mark>ECP is especially beneficial for patients who require long-term systemic therapy but need a treatment with a favorable safety profile and minimal immunosuppression.</mark>

---

### What is the optimal treatment schedule, and how long should ECP treatment be continued?

- **Initial induction phase**:  
  <mark>ECP is typically administered **twice weekly** (e.g., on two consecutive days every 2–3 weeks) for **6–12 months**, depending on clinical response.</mark>

- <mark>**Maintenance phase**:</mark>  
  <mark>After achieving a response (partial or complete), treatment frequency is gradually reduced based on clinical improvement and disease stability.</mark> <mark>Common regimens include:</mark>
  <mark>- Once every 2 weeks</mark>
  <mark>- Once monthly</mark>  
  <mark>Maintenance therapy is generally continued for **1–2 years or longer** in responders.</mark>

- <mark>**Duration of therapy**:</mark>  
  <mark>Treatment should be continued as long as there is **evidence of clinical benefit** and no disease progression.</mark> Some patients remain on long-term ECP for several years, especially those with chronic, relapsing disease.

- **Treatment adjustments**:  
  <mark>Frequency may be increased during disease flares or reduced in sustained remission.</mark> Individualization based on response, tolerability, and disease burden is key.

---

### How can therapeutic efficacy be assessed?

Therapeutic efficacy of ECP in CTCL should be evaluated using standardized response criteria, such as those defined by the **International Society for Cutaneous Lymphomas (ISCL)** and **European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC)**:

- **Skin assessment**:  
  Use of the **modified Severity-Weighted Assessment Tool (mSWAT)** to quantify skin lesion burden, including patches, plaques, and tumors.

- **Blood involvement**:  
  Evaluation of peripheral blood for Sézary cells using:
  - Absolute Sézary cell count
  - Flow cytometry for CD4+/CD7− or CD4+/CD26− phenotypes
  - T-cell receptor gene rearrangement (clonality)

- **Lymph nodes and visceral organs**:  
  Imaging (e.g., CT, PET-CT) and biopsies if indicated to assess nodal or internal organ involvement.

- **Response criteria**:
  - **Complete response (CR)**: Disappearance of all clinical, histologic, and laboratory signs of disease.
  - **Partial response (PR)**: ≥50% improvement in skin score (mSWAT), with improvement in other involved sites and no new lesions.
  - **Stable disease (SD)**: Less than PR but no progression.
  - **Progressive disease (PD)**: ≥25% increase in skin score or new lesions or worsening of blood/organ involvement.

- **Symptom assessment**:  
  Monitoring of **pruritus** (e.g., visual analog scale), quality of life (e.g., Skindex-16), and erythroderma.

- **Time to response**:  
  Responses may take **3–6 months** to become evident; therefore, treatment should generally continue for at least 6 months before assessing lack of efficacy.

Regular follow-up every 3 months during therapy is recommended to monitor response and adjust treatment accordingly.

# <mark>ICHTHYOSIS VULGARIS</mark>

<mark>Ichthyosis vulgaris (OMIM #146700), the most common form of ichthyosis, is typically mild.</mark> <mark>Although skin appears normal at birth, the condition usually becomes apparent within the first year of life.</mark> Scaling is most prominent on the extensor surfaces of the limbs, with relative sparing of flexural areas and the diaper region. <mark>The scales are often fine and white, covering large areas of the body.</mark>

<mark>On the lower extremities—frequently the most affected area—the scales may be centrally adherent with elevated edges, creating superficial fissures (cracking) in the stratum corneum.</mark> This gives the skin a rough texture.

## <mark>Associated Findings</mark>

<mark>Several additional features are commonly seen in ichthyosis vulgaris:</mark>

- <mark>**Hyperlinear palms**: Increased skin markings on the palms are typically present.</mark>
- <mark>**Palmar/plantar hyperkeratosis**: Some individuals exhibit thickening that may approach keratoderma.</mark>
- <mark>**Keratosis pilaris**: A follicular hyperkeratosis presenting as spine-like projections, commonly affecting the lateral arms, extensor thighs, and buttocks.</mark>
- **Atopy**: There is a strong association with atopic conditions such as eczema, asthma, and hay fever.
- **Hypohidrosis**: Rarely, reduced sweating may occur, leading to heat intolerance.

It is important to note that hyperlinear palms and keratosis pilaris can also be seen in individuals with atopy without ichthyosis vulgaris, which may complicate diagnosis.

## Clinical Variability and Environmental Influence

There is considerable variability in disease severity, even among affected members of the same family. Symptoms typically worsen in cold, dry climates and improve significantly in warm, humid environments—sometimes to the point of near-complete clearance.

## <mark>Genetics</mark>

<mark>Ichthyosis vulgaris is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the *FLG* gene, which encodes profilaggrin.</mark> Inheritance follows a **semi-dominant** pattern:

- **Homozygotes or compound heterozygotes** (mutations in both *FLG* alleles): exhibit a **severe phenotype**.
- **Heterozygotes** (mutation in one allele): present with a **milder phenotype**, with approximately **60% penetrance**.

The carrier frequency for *FLG* mutations is about **9%**, and the prevalence of homozygotes is estimated at **1 in 400** in the Anglo-European population.

## Diagnostic Challenges

- Mild ichthyosis vulgaris can be difficult to distinguish from simple **xerosis** (dry skin).
- Severe cases in males may resemble **X-linked recessive ichthyosis**, making clinical differentiation challenging without genetic testing.
- Histopathology (Fig. 47-2A) may show characteristic findings, but overlap with other conditions can occur.

Ongoing research continues to clarify the spectrum of *FLG*-related skin barrier dysfunction, ranging from mild dry skin to full-blown ichthyosis vulgaris.

# <mark>ICHTHYOSIS</mark>

# <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

<mark>A heterogeneous group of skin diseases characterized by generalized scaling and, often, areas of thickened skin.</mark>  
Most types are inherited and usually present at birth; however, some forms are acquired.  
Scales may vary in size, color, and distribution across the body.  
May be accompanied by erythema, abnormalities of the skin adnexa, and other cutaneous findings.  
Can be associated with systemic manifestations such as failure to thrive, increased susceptibility to infection, atopic dermatitis, neurosensory deafness, and neurologic disorders.  
Histopathology is typically non-specific, except in conditions such as epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, neutral lipid storage disease, Refsum disease, and acquired ichthyosis associated with sarcoidosis.

---

## <mark>OVERVIEW</mark>

Early reports of ichthyosis in Indian and Chinese medical literature date back several hundred years B.C. The condition was later described by Robert Willan in 1808.

Ichthyosis may present at birth or develop later in life. It can be limited to the skin or occur in association with abnormalities in other organ systems. While several well-defined types of ichthyosis can be reliably diagnosed based on clinical and genetic features, the significant clinical heterogeneity and the influence of environmental factors on scaling can make specific diagnosis challenging in some patients and families.

Siemens introduced genetic concepts into the classification of ichthyoses, laying the foundation for modern understanding.

Advances in genetic research have identified the underlying gene defects in many forms of ichthyosis—classified as genodermatoses. A new classification system is emerging, based on molecular and genetic etiologies. Identifying the mutated gene provides insight into the pathophysiologic mechanism, enabling more rational approaches to diagnosis, classification, and treatment.

Grouping these disorders by inheritance pattern (Table 47-1) and by underlying molecular abnormality (Table 47-2) enhances understanding of their clinical phenotypes and disease mechanisms. However, further research is needed to fully elucidate how specific gene mutations and protein disruptions lead to clinical disease, and to develop targeted, innovative therapies.

---

### TABLE 47-1  
**Features of Selected Ichthyoses**

| DIAGNOSIS | ONSET | CHARACTERISTIC CLINICAL FEATURES | ASSOCIATED FEATURES | GENE | PROTEIN | FUNCTION | SKIN HISTOPATHOLOGY |
|----------|-------|----------------------------------|----------------------|------|---------|----------|---------------------|
| **Autosomal semidominant** | | | | | | | |
| Ichthyosis vulgaris (OMIM #146700) | Infancy/childhood | Fine or centrally adherent scales with superficial fissuring; relative sparing of flexural areas; more severe on lower extremities; hyperlinear palms and soles | Keratosis pilaris; atopy | *FLG* | Absence of filaggrin | Uncertain | Hyperkeratosis; reduced or absent granular layer |
| **Autosomal dominant** | | | | | | | |
| EHK (bullous CIE; OMIM #113800) | Birth | Heterogeneous presentation | | | | | |

# <mark>CLINICAL PRESENTATION</mark>

A specific diagnosis in an individual or family with ichthyosis can help predict prognosis and is essential for genetic counseling. <mark>Several clinical features aid in distinguishing between different forms of ichthyosis, including:</mark>

- <mark>Age of onset</mark>  
- <mark>Presence of a collodion membrane at birth</mark>  
- Quality of scale (e.g., fine vs. coarse)  
- Presence or absence of erythroderma  
- <mark>Skin abnormalities in specific areas (e.g., palms, soles, ectropion, eclabium)</mark>  
- Adnexal involvement (e.g., alopecia, hair shaft abnormalities)  
- Extracutaneous manifestations or systemic involvement  

The appearance of the skin surface varies among types of ichthyosis. <mark>Visible scaling—ranging from fine to thick, plate-like flakes—may be present.</mark> Some patients exhibit thickened skin with or without obvious scaling. The term **hyperkeratosis** is used clinically to describe thickening of the stratum corneum, which may or may not be associated with visible scale.

A family pedigree can clarify the inheritance pattern. Parental consanguinity suggests autosomal recessive inheritance, although many autosomal dominant forms (e.g., **epidermolytic hyperkeratosis**) arise from spontaneous mutations, so a negative family history does not exclude this mode of inheritance.

Light microscopy is diagnostic in **epidermolytic hyperkeratosis**, showing characteristic cytoplasmic vacuolization and clumping of keratin filaments. Histopathology may also be helpful in select conditions such as **Refsum disease**, **neutral lipid storage disease**, and **acquired ichthyosis in sarcoidosis**. However, in many ichthyoses, histology lacks specificity. In such cases, genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis.

The development of ichthyosis in adulthood should prompt evaluation for underlying systemic disease, as it may be a cutaneous marker of malignancy, infection, or autoimmune disorders.

# ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS

The stratum corneum, the terminal product of epidermal differentiation, functions as a protective barrier. <mark>It consists of corneocytes ("bricks") embedded in a lipid-rich extracellular matrix ("mortar").</mark> Corneocytes are protein-dense, while the intercellular matrix is composed of hydrophobic lipid bilayers rich in ceramides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids.

The structural integrity and hydration of the skin depend on the corneocytes, whereas the lipid matrix is primarily responsible for the permeability barrier that prevents transepidermal water loss. Normally, desquamation occurs in a controlled, invisible process where individual corneocytes detach and shed singly.

In ichthyosis, this balance is disrupted. There is abnormal scale formation—both in quality and quantity—compromised barrier function, and altered epidermal kinetics. Hyperkeratosis results from either increased production of corneocytes, delayed desquamation, or both.

Epidermal differentiation involves multiple coordinated steps, and defects at various stages can lead to similar clinical phenotypes. <mark>Known genetic defects include:</mark>

- <mark>**Mutations in *KRT1* or *KRT10***: Cause **epidermolytic hyperkeratosis**, characterized by abnormal keratin filament assembly and cytolysis in the suprabasal layers.</mark>
- <mark>**Mutations in *TGM1***: Encode transglutaminase 1, an enzyme critical for cross-linking the cornified envelope and attaching ceramides. Deficiency leads to **lamellar ichthyosis**, a severe form of autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI).</mark>
- <mark>**Deficiency of steroid sulfatase**: Results in **X-linked recessive ichthyosis**, where impaired hydrolysis of cholesterol sulfate disrupts corneocyte desquamation, leading to scale accumulation.</mark>

<mark>These molecular insights underscore the complexity of epidermal differentiation and highlight how disruptions in structural proteins, enzymes, or lipid metabolism can converge on a common clinical phenotype—ichthyosis.</mark>

## <mark>Predominant comedonal acne</mark>

<mark>Topical treatment with either a retinoid, azelaic acid, or salicylic acid is recommended as a first-line approach for patients with predominant comedonal facial acne without significant inflammatory lesions.</mark> <mark>Topical retinoids are considered more effective than azelaic acid, which in turn is more effective than salicylic acid.</mark> <mark>Topical retinoids and azelaic acid inhibit the formation of microcomedones—the precursor to all acne lesions—and are both comedolytic and anti-comedogenic, with additional anti-inflammatory properties.</mark> <mark>Retinoid-based therapy is recommended as a first-line treatment for almost all acne patients by the Global Alliance.</mark>

<mark>The dose or frequency of application of first-line treatments may be reduced if patients experience adverse events such as skin irritation.</mark>

### Maintenance therapy

<mark>Maintenance therapy with a topical retinoid or azelaic acid is recommended once a patient has responded to treatment and is clear or nearly clear of acne.</mark> <mark>The goal is to prevent recurrence by suppressing microcomedone formation, which can persist in clinically normal-appearing skin.</mark> <mark>Retinoids are generally preferred over azelaic acid due to stronger evidence of efficacy, although recent data suggest that azelaic acid and adapalene have comparable effectiveness in adult female acne.</mark>

Dose or frequency should be reduced if irritation occurs. Salicylic acid at concentrations >5% for over 12 weeks or 10% for over 6 weeks is not recommended for maintenance due to potential systemic toxicity. Benzoyl peroxide (BPO) monotherapy should not be used for maintenance because it does not effectively target microcomedones or comedones. Topical antibiotic monotherapy is also not recommended, as long-term use may promote antibiotic-resistant *Cutibacterium acnes*.

## Predominant papulopustular acne

For patients with predominant papulopustular acne, disease severity should be classified as:

- **Mild**: Grades 1–2  
- **Moderate**: Grade 3  
- **Severe**: Grades 4–5  

### Mild papulopustular acne (grades 1–2)

<mark>First-line topical treatments include:</mark>
- <mark>Benzoyl peroxide (BPO)</mark>
- <mark>Second-generation retinoids (e.g., adapalene)</mark>
- <mark>Azelaic acid</mark>

<mark>Alternatively, fixed-dose combination therapies may be used, such as:</mark>
- <mark>Clindamycin 1% / tretinoin 0.025%</mark>
- <mark>Adapalene 0.1% / BPO 2.5%</mark>
- <mark>Clindamycin 1% / BPO 3% or 5%</mark>

The choice of agent should be individualized based on patient characteristics, tolerability, and preferences.

### Moderate papulopustular acne (grade 3 to 4)

Topical fixed-dose combination therapies are recommended as the preferred first-line approach.

## When to Use Topical vs. Oral Therapy in Acne

As shown in Fig. <mark>17, **topical therapy** is first-line for patients with **mild-to-moderate acne**.</mark> <mark>Several factors influence the decision to initiate **systemic therapy**, including:</mark>

- <mark>Degree of inflammation</mark>  
- <mark>Truncal involvement</mark>  
- <mark>Duration of acne</mark>  
- <mark>Decreased quality of life</mark>  
- <mark>Presence or risk of scarring</mark>  

<mark>Early, effective treatment is crucial, as the risk of scarring increases with delayed intervention.</mark> Topical therapy is also ideal for **maintenance treatment** and should include a **retinoid** with or without **benzoyl peroxide (BPO)**, or **azelaic acid**—particularly in patients who are pregnant or planning pregnancy.

---

## Systemic Acne Treatment

<mark>Evidence-based systemic treatments for acne include:</mark>

- <mark>**Oral tetracyclines** (used in combination with topical agents such as retinoids, azelaic acid, and BPO)</mark>  
- <mark>**Oral isotretinoin**</mark>  
- <mark>**Anti-androgenic pills**</mark>  

**Zinc** may benefit patients with confirmed deficiency. However, excessive intake of zinc (and selenium) can lead to adverse effects. Zinc supplementation may be considered during pregnancy as a supportive measure.  

**Biologics** and **non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)** lack strong evidence for efficacy in acne, although specific agents like **zileuton** have shown effectiveness in some studies.

---

### <mark>Oral Antibiotics</mark>

<mark>Antibiotics have long been a cornerstone of acne management.</mark> <mark>However, growing concerns about **antibiotic resistance** and national and international efforts to promote **antibiotic stewardship** have led experts to advocate for **antibiotic-sparing strategies**.</mark>

<mark>Effective oral antibiotics for acne include:</mark>

- <mark>**Tetracyclines**: tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, lymecycline</mark>  
- <mark>**Trimethoprim ± sulfamethoxazole**</mark>  
- <mark>**Macrolides**: erythromycin, azithromycin</mark>  
- <mark>**Amoxicillin**, **cephalexin**</mark>  

<mark>**Tetracyclines** are first-line for **moderate-to-severe acne**, unless contraindicated.</mark> <mark>**Macrolides** are an alternative when tetracyclines are unsuitable.</mark> <mark>**Penicillins and cephalosporins** have limited supporting data but may be used in pregnancy or in patients with allergies to other antibiotic classes.</mark>

<mark>Oral antibiotics primarily exert **anti-inflammatory effects**, with secondary activity against *Cutibacterium acnes*.</mark> <mark>They should be prescribed for **no longer than 3 months** to minimize the risk of microbial resistance.</mark> <mark>Prolonged use should be avoided.</mark>

<mark>According to the **American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) guidelines**, oral antibiotics are indicated for **moderate-to-severe inflammatory acne** and **must be combined** with **topical retinoids and BPO** to enhance efficacy and reduce resistance.</mark>

Prescribing practices in the **Middle East** are largely based on clinical judgment due to limited regional data. Additionally, there is a lack of structured **antibiotic stewardship** and educational programs in dermatology.

---

### Hormonal Therapy

Hormonal therapy can be an effective option for **women with acne**, particularly those with hormonal imbalances or signs of hyperandrogenism. However, cultural and societal norms in the Middle East may create barriers to discussing or prescribing **estrogen-containing combined oral contraceptives (COCs)**, especially for unmarried or young women.

Dermatologists are encouraged to become familiar with available hormonal options and consider **collaborating with gynecologists** when appropriate.

Hormonal therapy should **not be used as monotherapy**, as its onset of action is slow. Initial improvements typically include:

- Reduction in **comedones**  
- Decreased **seborrhea**  
- Improvement in **inflammatory lesions** after 8–10 weeks  

Both the **European Dermatology Forum (EDF)** and **AAD guidelines** recommend hormonal therapy as an adjunctive treatment for women with acne.

---

### Table 10: American Academy of Dermatology Recommendations for Oral Antibiotics in Acne

Systemic antibiotics are recommended for:

- **Moderate and severe acne**

## Thyroid Hormone Physiology and Regulation

<mark>Thyroid hormones act on target tissues by activating cytoplasmic receptors that subsequently translocate to the nucleus and activate specific thyroid-responsive genes.</mark> <mark>Thyroid hormone synthesis is heavily dependent on iodine, and changes in iodine intake can result in either hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism.</mark>

### Regulation of Thyroid Hormone Synthesis

<mark>Synthesis of thyroid hormone is regulated by the pituitary gland through the release of **thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)**, which is itself stimulated by **thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH)** from the hypothalamus.</mark> <mark>TSH acts on the thyroid gland by binding to a G-protein-coupled receptor (TSH-R), triggering thyroid hormone synthesis and release.</mark>

<mark>Aberrant activation of TSH-R underlies the hyperthyroidism seen in **Graves disease**, where nearly all patients have **long-acting thyroid stimulator (LATS) autoantibodies** that bind and activate the TSH-R.</mark> <mark>TRH also acts via a G-protein-coupled receptor, and administration of recombinant TRH followed by measurement of TSH response can help distinguish between primary (thyroidal) and central (hypothalamic-pituitary) causes of hypothyroidism.</mark>

### <mark>Feedback Regulation</mark>

<mark>Circulating levels of **thyroxine (T₄)** and **triiodothyronine (T₃)** tightly regulate the release of both TSH and TRH through negative feedback mechanisms.</mark> <mark>Persistent stimulation of the thyroid gland can lead to **goiter**, a hypertrophy of the gland.</mark>

### <mark>Thyroid Hormone Transport and Availability</mark>

<mark>The majority of thyroid hormones in the blood are bound to plasma proteins:</mark>
- <mark>**Thyroid-binding globulin (TBG)** – the primary binding protein</mark>
- <mark>**Transthyretin** (formerly prealbumin)</mark>
- <mark>**Albumin**</mark>

<mark>Various medical conditions and medications can alter the levels of these binding proteins or affect the peripheral conversion of T₄ to T₃—the biologically active form responsible for most of thyroid hormone’s effects.</mark> <mark>These changes can influence tissue availability of thyroid hormone independently of thyroid synthesis.</mark>

<mark>Thyroid hormone levels may also be affected by several medications, including those commonly prescribed by dermatologists.</mark>

### Classification of Hyperthyroidism

Hyperthyroidism can be classified based on **radioiodine uptake**:
- **High uptake**: indicates increased thyroid hormone synthesis (e.g., Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter)
- **Low or absent uptake**: suggests either an extrathyroidal source of hormone or destruction of thyroid tissue with release of preformed hormone (e.g., thyroiditis)

Genetic predisposition and environmental factors, such as infection, are believed to contribute to the development of autoimmune thyroid diseases.

In **toxic adenoma**, molecular studies have identified frequent activating mutations in the **TSH-R**, leading to constitutive (TSH-independent) stimulation of thyroid hormone production.

### Cutaneous Manifestations of Thyroid Disease

While some skin findings in hyperthyroidism are indirect, most cutaneous manifestations result from the **direct effects of thyroid hormones** on:
- Keratinized epithelium (epidermis, hair, nails)
- Stromal cells in the dermis

Thyroid hormones are essential for optimal **epidermal proliferation** in both in vitro and in vivo settings. They regulate genes involved in **keratinocyte proliferation** and stimulate the expression of specific **keratins**, influencing skin, hair, and nail health.

# <mark>Cutaneous and Systemic Manifestations of Hypothyroidism</mark>

<mark>The skin in hypothyroidism is typically **xerotic**, with a poorly hydrated **stratum corneum**.</mark> <mark>Histologically, the epidermis is thin, showing **hyperkeratosis** and **follicular plugging**.</mark> These changes are generalized in distribution, which helps differentiate them from conditions such as **atopic dermatitis** and **keratosis pilaris**, which predominantly affect the extremities. <mark>Additionally, a **fine wrinkling** of the skin may be observed.</mark>

<mark>A distinctive **yellow-orange discoloration** of the skin—known as **carotenemia**—can occur due to accumulation of $\beta$-carotene in the stratum corneum.</mark> This is likely secondary to reduced hepatic conversion of $\beta$-carotene to vitamin A in the setting of hypothyroidism, leading to increased circulating carotene levels.

## Myxedema

**Myxedema** is the hallmark cutaneous finding in hypothyroidism and is distinct from the dermopathy associated with Graves disease. It results from dermal deposition of **mucopolysaccharides**, particularly **hyaluronic acid** and **chondroitin sulfate**. This accumulation leads to skin that is **doughy, swollen, and waxy**, without pitting edema. Myxedema is typically generalized but may be more pronounced in the extremities.

<mark>With treatment of the underlying hypothyroidism, myxedema tends to resolve.</mark>

### Characteristic Facial Features
- **Broadened nose**
- **Thickened lips**
- **Puffy eyelids**
- **Macroglossia** (enlarged, smooth, clumsy tongue)
- **Loss of facial expression** (a pathognomonic feature)

### Cutaneous Findings in Hypothyroidism
- Doughy, dry skin with fine wrinkling  
- Yellow-orange carotenemia  
- Dry, brittle hair with slow growth  
- Brittle nails with longitudinal and transverse striations  
- Impaired wound healing  

### Hair Changes
- Hair becomes **coarse, dry, and brittle**
- **Diffuse or patchy scalp hair loss**
- Increased proportion of hair follicles in the **telogen phase**
- **Telogen effluvium** may occur following acute onset
- **Loss of the outer third of the eyebrows** (see Fig. 152-12)
- While body hair may be reduced, there can be paradoxical increase in **lanugo-type hair** on the back, shoulders, and extremities

### Nail and Oral Findings
- Nails grow slowly and may become **thickened, brittle**, and show **longitudinal or transverse ridges**
- **Macroglossia** contributes to a large, smooth, red, and clumsy tongue
- Hoarseness may occur due to **recurrent laryngeal nerve compression** in patients with goiter

### Goiter-Related Complications
- Large goiters can cause **tracheal or esophageal displacement**
- **Retrosternal goiters** may lead to **Pemberton’s sign**: facial plethora and jugular venous distention when arms are raised above the head, indicating thoracic inlet obstruction

## <mark>Diagnosis</mark>
- <mark>**Serum thyrotropin (TSH)** is the best initial test</mark>
- <mark>Additional tests: **free triiodothyronine (T3)** and **free thyroxine (T4)**</mark>

## <mark>Management</mark>
- **Endocrine consultation** recommended
- **Oral thyroxine replacement** (typically 75–150 μg/day)
- **Careful monitoring** for coexisting heart, lung, or adrenal disease

## <mark>Treatment of Severe Nodular/Conglobate Acne</mark>

### <mark>High Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Oral isotretinoin** is strongly recommended as monotherapy for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne due to its superior efficacy compared to systemic antibiotics or topical therapy alone.</mark>

### <mark>Medium Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic antibiotics** in combination with the fixed-dose combination of **adapalene and benzoyl peroxide (BPO)**, or with **azelaic acid**, can be recommended for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>

### <mark>Low Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic antibiotics** in combination with **adapalene** or **BPO** can be considered for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>
- <mark>For females: **Hormonal anti-androgens** in combination with systemic antibiotics and topical treatments (excluding topical antibiotics) can be considered.</mark>
- <mark>For females: **Hormonal anti-androgens** in combination with a topical treatment (excluding antibiotics) can also be considered.</mark>

### <mark>Open Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>Due to insufficient evidence, no recommendation can be made for or against the use of **intense pulsed light (IPL)** or **laser therapy** in severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>
- <mark>Although **photodynamic therapy (PDT)** shows effectiveness, it cannot currently be recommended due to lack of standardized treatment protocols and concerns about acute adverse reactions.</mark>

### <mark>Negative Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Topical monotherapy** is not recommended for conglobate acne.</mark>
- <mark>**Oral antibiotics** are not recommended as monotherapy.</mark>
- <mark>**Oral anti-androgens** are not recommended as monotherapy.</mark>
- <mark>**Artificial UV radiation sources** are not recommended.</mark>
- <mark>**Visible light therapy** as monotherapy is not recommended.</mark>

---

## <mark>Choice of Topical vs. Systemic Treatment</mark>

<mark>There is limited evidence directly comparing topical and systemic therapies or evaluating the added benefit of combination therapy over topical treatment alone.</mark> <mark>Most studies compare topical antibiotic monotherapy with systemic antibiotic monotherapy.</mark>

<mark>In clinical practice, expert consensus supports that:</mark>
- <mark>Patients with **severe papulopustular acne** or **moderate nodular acne** achieve better outcomes with **systemic antibiotic plus topical treatment**, or with **systemic isotretinoin**.</mark>
- <mark>Involvement of the trunk is a key factor favoring systemic therapy.</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic treatments** are associated with better adherence and higher patient satisfaction, particularly in widespread disease.</mark>

---

## <mark>Additional Considerations</mark>

- <mark>**Isotretinoin** is highly effective in severe cases, supported by strong clinical experience despite limited controlled trial data specific to nodular/conglobate forms.</mark>
- <mark>Evidence for many treatment options was downgraded due to reliance on indirect data from studies of severe papulopustular acne, particularly when assessing nodule and cyst reduction.</mark>
- <mark>Prescribers should be mindful of the risk of **antibiotic resistance** when using systemic antibiotics.</mark>
- <mark>Systemic antibiotics such as **doxycycline** and **lymecycline** should be limited to a maximum treatment duration of **3 months**.</mark>
- <mark>In cases where higher-strength recommendations cannot be followed (due to cost, availability, licensing, or legal restrictions), lower-strength alternatives may be used as first-line therapy.</mark>

---

## Treatment of Papulopustular Acne

There is insufficient evidence to recommend laser or light-based therapies (other than blue light) for papulopustular acne due to lack of standardized protocols, clinical trial data, and real-world experience.

Systemic treatment with **isotretinoin** is recommended in severe cases based on high efficacy observed in clinical practice, although safety and tolerability data remain limited and insufficient for guiding recommendations independently.

# A Consensus-Based Practical and Daily Guide for the Treatment of Acne Patients

## Abstract

**Background**  
Many current guidelines provide detailed evidence-based recommendations for acne treatment.

**Objective**  
To create consensus-based, simple, easy-to-use algorithms for clinical acne treatment in daily office-based practice and to provide checklists to assist in determining why a patient may not have responded to treatment and what action to take.

**Methods**  
Existing treatment guidelines and consensus papers were reviewed. The information was extracted and simplified according to daily clinical practice needs using a consensus-based approach and based on the authors' clinical expertise.

**Results**  
Separate simple algorithms are presented for the treatment of:
- <mark>Predominant comedonal acne</mark>
- <mark>Predominant papulopustular acne</mark>
- <mark>Nodular/conglobate acne</mark>

- **Comedonal acne**: Initial treatment with topical retinoid, azelaic acid, or salicylic acid.
- **Papulopustular acne**: Fixed-combination topicals recommended, with therapy tailored to disease severity.
- **Nodular/conglobate acne**: Oral isotretinoin or fixed combinations plus oral antibiotics (in men); in women, these may be supplemented with oral anti-androgenic hormonal therapy.

Treatment response should be evaluated:
- **8 weeks** after initiation for comedonal or papulopustular acne
- **12 weeks** after initiation for nodular/conglobate acne

Once clear or almost clear, **maintenance therapy** with a topical retinoid or azelaic acid is recommended to prevent recurrence.

Reasons for lack of treatment response fall into five categories:
1. Disease progression  
2. Non-drug-related reasons  
3. Drug-related reasons  
4. Poor adherence  
5. Adverse events  

**Conclusion**  
This practical guide provides dermatologists with simple, clinically applicable treatment algorithms tailored to different acne types. The included checklists for evaluating treatment failure facilitate effective management in daily practice.

---

## Introduction

Acne is a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit, commonly affecting adolescents and imposing a significant psychosocial and physical burden. The primary pathogenic factors include:
- Increased sebum production  
- Abnormal keratinization  
- Colonization by *Cutibacterium acnes* (formerly *Propionibacterium acnes*)  
- Inflammatory response mediated by innate immunity  

Due to this multifactorial pathophysiology, effective treatment typically requires combination therapy targeting multiple pathways.

Clinically, acne presents in various forms. This article focuses on three main types:
1. **Predominant comedonal facial acne**  
2. **Predominant papulopustular facial acne**  
3. **Nodular and/or conglobate acne** (affecting face, trunk, and upper limbs)

While numerous national and international guidelines offer evidence-based recommendations, there remains a need for simplified, practical tools that can be easily applied in routine clinical settings. 

This article presents:
- Consensus-based treatment algorithms for the three main acne types  
- Checklists to identify causes of treatment failure  
- Guidance on next steps when response is inadequate  

Special populations such as infants, adult women with hormonal acne, and syndromic acne are not addressed here.

---

## Methods

The treatment algorithms were developed by a panel of 17 acne experts. The process involved:
- Review of key international, evidence-based acne guidelines, including those from:
  - Global Alliance to Improve Outcomes in Acne  
  - European Dermatology Forum  
  - American Academy of Dermatology  
  - Asian expert groups  

The data from these sources were synthesized, simplified, and adapted to reflect real-world clinical practice through expert consensus and clinical experience. Recent literature was also considered to support recommendations.

---

## <mark>Results</mark>

### <mark>Treatment Algorithms</mark>

<mark>For ease of use in daily practice, separate algorithms are provided for:</mark>

#### <mark>1. Predominant Comedonal Acne</mark>
<mark>**First-line treatment:**</mark>
- <mark>Topical retinoid</mark>  
- <mark>Azelaic acid</mark>  
- <mark>Salicylic acid</mark>  

<mark>These agents normalize follicular keratinization and prevent comedone formation.</mark>

#### <mark>2. Predominant Papulopustular Acne</mark>
<mark>**Recommended:**</mark>
- <mark>Fixed-combination topical therapies (e.g., benzoyl peroxide + antibiotic, retinoid + benzoyl peroxide, or retinoid + antibiotic)</mark>  
- <mark>Therapy should be adjusted based on severity</mark>

<mark>Combination products improve efficacy and reduce antibiotic resistance risk.</mark>

#### <mark>3. Nodular/Conglobate Acne</mark>
<mark>**Treatment options:**</mark>
- <mark>**Oral isotretinoin** – first-line for severe nodular or conglobate acne</mark>  
- <mark>**Fixed combinations + oral antibiotics** – alternative in men if isotretinoin is contraindicated or declined</mark>  
- <mark>**In women**: Consider adding **oral anti-androgenic hormonal therapy** (e.g., combined oral contraceptives, spironolactone) as adjunctive treatment</mark>

### Evaluation of Treatment Response

Assessment should be performed using the **Global Evaluation Acne (GEA) scale**.

- **Clinical improvement**: Reduction of at least one to two grades on the GEA scale  
- **Timing of evaluation**:
  - **8 weeks** for comedonal and papulopustular acne  
  - **12 weeks** for nodular/conglobate acne  

### Maintenance Therapy

Once a patient is clear or almost clear:
- Initiate **maintenance therapy** with:
  - Topical retinoid  
  - Or azelaic acid  
- Purpose: Prevent recurrence by maintaining follicular patency and reducing inflammation

### Checklist: Causes of Treatment Failure

When a patient fails to respond, consider the following five categories:

1. **Disease progression**  
   - Natural course of acne may worsen before improving  
   - Consider escalation of therapy if progression occurs

2. **Non-drug-related reasons**  
   - Hormonal fluctuations (e.g., menstrual cycle, PCOS)  
   - Lifestyle factors (diet, stress, skincare practices)  
   - Cosmetic product use (comedogenic ingredients)

3. **Drug-related reasons**  
   - Inappropriate choice of agent for acne type/severity  
   - Suboptimal dosing or formulation  
   - Drug interactions

4. **Poor adherence**  
   - Common due to complex regimens, side effects, or lack of immediate results  
   - Simplify regimen, educate patient, and assess understanding

5. **Adverse events**  
   - Irritation, dryness, or allergic reactions may limit use  
   - Adjust formulation, frequency, or switch agents

For each identified cause, appropriate corrective actions should be taken, such as modifying treatment, improving patient education, or switching therapies.

--- 

*Note: Figures and tables referenced (e.g., Fig. 1–4, Table 1) are not included in this text version.*

## <mark>Acne Classification and Management Overview</mark>

### <mark>Clinical Presentation of Acne</mark>
- **(bii)** Acute papulopustular acne with small nodules (<0.5–1.0 cm).  
- <mark>**(c)** Severe papulopustular acne progressing to conglobate acne, characterized by sinus tract formation and deep scarring.</mark>  
- <mark>**(d)** Conglobate acne affecting the trunk.</mark>

### Treatment Follow-Up and Response Evaluation
Regular follow-up for individual acne treatments is essential to assess therapeutic efficacy in relation to the degree of inflammation and scarring potential. In more complex cases, treatment response may be delayed. Patients should be advised to seek earlier medical review if they experience adverse effects or poor tolerability.

In cases of treatment failure, the dermatologist should investigate potential causes. The current guidelines provide practical checklists (referenced in Tables 2–4) outlining common reasons for lack of response and recommended next steps.

### Global Evaluation Acne (GEA) Scale for Facial Acne

| Grade | Severity       | Description |
|-------|----------------|-------------|
| 0     | Clear          | No lesions; residual pigmentation or erythema may be present |
| 1     | Almost clear   | Very few scattered comedones and minimal papules |
| 2     | Mild           | Less than half the face involved; few comedones, papules, and pustules |
| 3     | Moderate       | More than half the face involved; numerous comedones, papules, and pustules; possibly one nodule |
| 4     | Severe         | Entire face involved; widespread papules, pustules, comedones; rare nodules |
| 5     | Very severe    | Extensive inflammatory lesions with nodules covering the face |

### General Skin Care Recommendations
All acne patients should incorporate the following into their daily skin care routine:
- Use of broad-spectrum **anti-UVA and UVB sunscreen**  
- Gentle **cleansers with a skin-friendly pH**  
- **Non-comedogenic moisturizers**

These measures support overall acne management and help maintain skin barrier integrity.
